questions.q: The original National Programme for Control of Blindness (NPCB) began in ___; it became NPCBVI in 2017.
questions.exp: NPCB started in 1976 and was amended to NPCBVI in 2017. (Book p223)

questions.q: Clinical blindness is defined as:
questions.exp: The clinical definition given is no perception of light. (Book p223)

questions.q: Under NPCBVI/WHO, blindness is presenting VA below 3/60 in the better eye with best correction OR visual field below ___ degrees from fixation.
questions.exp: The definition is presenting VA <3/60 in the better eye with best possible correction or visual-field limitation to <10° from fixation. (Book p223)

questions.q: Which ordered visual-acuity bands correctly describe severe, moderate and early visual impairment?
questions.exp: NPCBVI categories in the better eye with available correction: blindness <3/60, severe VI <6/60–3/60, moderate VI <6/18–6/60, early VI <6/12–6/18. (Book p223)

questions.q: A person has VA <6/18 or field <10° from the fovea and can potentially use vision to plan or execute a task. This meets the listed description of:
questions.exp: Functional low vision is VA <6/18 or field <10° from fovea with ability/potential to use vision for a task; the table also defines BCVA/pinhole blindness as best-corrected <3/60. (Book p223)

questions.q: The 2015-19 National Blindness and Visual Impairment Survey reported blindness prevalence of ___ in 2019.
questions.exp: The recent-facts note gives blindness prevalence as 0.36% in 2019. (Book p223)

questions.q: The program goal is to reduce avoidable blindness prevalence to below ___ by 2025.
questions.exp: The listed goal is <0.25% avoidable blindness by 2025. (Book p223)

questions.q: For blindness, which cause ranking is shown for age >=50 versus age 0-49?
opts: >=50: amblyopia then refractive error; 0-49: cataract then glaucoma
>=50: glaucoma then cataract; 0-49: refractive error then trauma
>=50: cataract then corneal opacity; 0-49: corneal opacity then amblyopia
>=50: corneal opacity then cataract; 0-49: amblyopia then cataract
questions.exp: At >=50, cataract is most common (66.2%) and corneal opacity second (8.2%); at 0-49, corneal opacity is most common (37.5%) and amblyopia second (25%). (Book p224)

questions.q: Which visual-impairment cause ranking is correct for older versus younger age groups?
opts: >=50: refractive errors then cataract; 0-49: cataract then glaucoma
>=50: cataract then refractive errors; 0-49: refractive errors then cataract
>=50: corneal opacity then glaucoma; 0-49: amblyopia then cataract
>=50: cataract then corneal opacity; 0-49: glaucoma then refractive errors
questions.exp: For visual impairment, >=50: cataract 71.2% then refractive error 13.4%; age 0-49: refractive error 29.6% then cataract 25%. (Book p224)

questions.q: Vision 2020 launched in Geneva in 1999 and was adopted by India in ___ at Goa.
questions.exp: Vision 2020 launched in 1999 in Geneva and India adopted it in 2001 at Goa. (Book p224)

questions.q: One stated Vision 2020 aim was to reduce the number of blind people to ___ million by 2020.
questions.exp: The stated aims were to reduce blind people to 25 million by 2020 and eliminate avoidable blindness. (Book p224)

questions.q: Which condition appears among India's Vision 2020 priorities but not the listed global five?
questions.exp: India's list includes cataract, refractive errors, childhood blindness, endemic trachoma, glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy and corneal blindness; global list includes the first four and onchocerciasis. (Book p224)

questions.q: Match Vision 2020 centre tier with approximate number — 1) Apex  2) Centre of excellence  3) Training centre  4) Service centre  5) Vision centre … A) 200  B) 20,000  C) 2  D) 2,000  E) 20
questions.exp: The pyramid lists 2 apexes, one per 500 million population. (Book p225)

questions.q: Professional leadership, CME/research, quality assurance and strategy development are functions of the:
questions.exp: The centre of excellence is assigned leadership, CME/research, standards/QA and strategy development. (Book p225)

questions.q: Which tier and service are paired correctly?
opts: Vision centre: retinal surgery and corneal transplantation
Training centre: tertiary eye care and surgical training at a medical-college ophthalmology department
Service centre: school screening by a paramedic
questions.exp: Training centres are ophthalmology departments of medical colleges, providing tertiary eye care (retinal, corneal and glaucoma surgery) and training/CME. (Book p225)

questions.q: A service centre is staffed by an ophthalmologist and provides common eye surgery, refraction and:
questions.exp: Service centres provide cataract/other common surgery, refraction and referral services; ratio 1 per 500,000. (Book p225)

questions.q: Vision centres provide primary eye care and school screening; the listed provider is a:
questions.exp: Vision centres provide refraction/glasses, primary eye care and screening/referral, performed by a paramedic ophthalmic assistant. (Book p225)

questions.q: The school eye-screening programme targets children in classes ___, usually aged 10-14 years.
questions.exp: The target is classes V-VIII (10-14 years); one teacher screens about 150 students. (Book p225)

questions.q: A school-screening child has VA <6/9 in either eye. The listed next step is referral to the nearest:
questions.exp: Vision screening cards and a measurement tape are used, VA is recorded and a child with VA <6/9 in either eye is referred to the nearest PHC. (Book p225)

questions.q: Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK) operates under the:
questions.exp: RBSK is launched under the National Health Mission and covers screening/early intervention from birth to 18 years. (Book p226)

questions.q: The RBSK 4 Ds are defects at birth, diseases, deficiencies and:
questions.exp: RBSK screens the 4 Ds: defects at birth, diseases, deficiencies and developmental delays. (Book p226)

questions.q: Which set contains only listed congenital/birth defects screened under RBSK?
opts: Age-related cataract, diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma and trachoma
Dry eye, pterygium, keratoconus and uveitis
Congenital cataract, retinopathy of prematurity, neural-tube defect and congenital heart disease
Myopia, optic neuritis, AMD and retinal detachment
questions.exp: Birth defects include neural-tube defect, Down syndrome, cleft lip/palate, talipes, developmental dysplasia of hip, congenital cataract/deafness/heart disease and ROP. (Book p226)

questions.q: Which list is made up of RBSK deficiency conditions?
opts: Otitis media, dental caries, scabies and convulsions
Severe anaemia, vitamin A deficiency, vitamin D deficiency, severe acute malnutrition and goitre
Autism, ADHD, language delay and hearing impairment
Cleft palate, talipes, ROP and congenital cataract
questions.exp: Deficiencies include severe anaemia, vitamin A deficiency (Bitot spot), vitamin D deficiency (rickets), severe acute malnutrition and goitre. (Book p226)

questions.q: Which collection belongs to the childhood-disease group in RBSK?
opts: Skin conditions, otitis media, rheumatic heart disease, reactive airway disease, dental caries and convulsive disorders
Cleft lip, Down syndrome, talipes and ROP
Anaemia, goitre, rickets and Bitot spots
Autism, ADHD, hearing loss and motor delay
questions.exp: The childhood-disease list includes skin conditions (scabies/fungal infection/eczema), otitis media, rheumatic heart disease, reactive airway disease, dental caries and convulsive disorders. (Book p226)

questions.q: Which is listed under developmental delays, with congenital hypothyroidism/sickle cell/beta thalassemia marked optional?
questions.exp: Developmental delays include vision/hearing impairment, neuromotor/motor/cognitive/language delay, autism, learning disorder and ADHD; congenital hypothyroidism, sickle cell anaemia and beta thalassemia are optional. (Book p226)

questions.q: Tuberculosis and leprosy appear in the RBSK list but are noted as not specific to children.
questions.exp: The page brackets tuberculosis and leprosy as conditions not specific to children. (Book p226)

questions.q: Match the RBSK screening category with age, approximate coverage and provider — newborns; preschool; school children.
opts: Birth-6 weeks / 17 crore / teacher; 6 weeks-6 years / 2 crore / mobile team; 6-18 / 8 crore / ANM
Birth-6 weeks / 2 crore / mobile team; 6 weeks-6 years / 8 crore / Anganwadi + ANM; 6-18 years / 17 crore / school-district hospital questionnaires
Birth-6 years / 2 crore / district hospital; 6-18 / 8 crore / mobile team; preschool / 17 crore / teacher
Birth-6 weeks / 8 crore / ANM; preschool / 17 crore / district hospital; school / 2 crore / mobile team
questions.exp: Newborns (birth-6 weeks): 2 crores, mobile health team; preschool (6 weeks-6 years): 8 crores, Anganwadi/ANM; school (6-18): 17 crores, district-hospital-supported school questionnaires. (Book p227)

questions.q: For a child aged 0-6 years needing RBSK intervention, referral is through the:
opts: District Early Intervention Center (DEIC) to an appropriate tertiary centre
questions.exp: For ages 0-6, intervention is via DEIC with referral to an appropriate tertiary centre; for 6-18 years, use an existing public health facility. (Book p227)

questions.q: RBSK intervention for ages 6-18 years is provided through an:
questions.exp: The listed route is DEIC/tertiary referral for ages 0-6 and existing public health facility for ages 6-18. (Book p227)

units.title: NPCBVI definitions and blindness indicators
units.guide: NPCB became NPCBVI in 2017. Distinguish clinical blindness from program/WHO definitions and the visual-impairment bands; learn survey prevalence and the avoidable-blindness target.

units.title: Causes of blindness and Vision 2020
units.guide: Know age-stratified blindness and visual-impairment causes, Vision 2020 dates and aims, and the differing India/global priority-disease lists.

units.title: Vision 2020 service pyramid and school screening
units.guide: The Vision 2020 pyramid scales apex, excellence, training, service and vision centres by population served, workforce and services. School screening targets class V-VIII and refers reduced acuity to PHC.

units.title: RBSK: aims, 4 Ds and screened conditions
units.guide: RBSK under NHM provides screening/early intervention from birth to 18 years. Its 4 Ds organize birth defects, diseases, deficiencies and developmental delays; know the eye-relevant birth-defect and vision-impairment entries among the broader list.

units.title: RBSK screening pathways and intervention
units.guide: RBSK groups screening by age and setting: newborns, preschool children and school children. Know coverage estimates, responsible screeners and the intervention destination for ages 0-6 versus 6-18.
